Here are my verse-by-verse notes for Ecclesiastes 3, drawn from the sources I was able to access and read in full. (Due to search and fetch limits, I was unable to reach Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist/Wesleyan, or modern scholarship sites directly. I note this where relevant.)

---

## Ecclesiastes 3 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: “To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven”

- **The key assertion: God's sovereignty over all time and events.** Solomon teaches that there is a God-appointed time for every moment; the Lord is ultimately in control of all human affairs. The Hebrew word for "season" (*zeman*) denotes a fixed, definite portion of time, while "time" (*eth*) refers to the beginning of a period or time in general. Every event under heaven is a "purpose-driven activity," not a random happening. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-3-commentary)
- **Gill** adds that God has foreordained all things — the rise and fall of kingdoms, the state of the church, even the day of Christ's return — and fixed the duration and end of all things. Nothing happens sooner or later than God wills. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)
- **Ellicott** notes that "purpose" (*chephets*) primarily means "pleasure" or "desire" in earlier Hebrew, but takes the general sense of "a matter" in later Hebrew. Providence arranges the moment when everything shall happen, its duration, and the time appropriate to it. The writer does not yet attempt to reconcile free-will and God's decree. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/3.htm)
- **Enduring Word** adds that the repeated refrain "a time… a time…" conveys not celebration of variety but the oppressive monotony of life's cycles (citing Morgan and Kidner). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)
- The NET Bible note (cited by Precept Austin) observes that vv.1–8 refer to God's appointed timetable for human activities, while vv.9–15 state God is ultimately responsible for the timing of all events — a balance between divine sovereignty and human responsibility. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-3-commentary)

### v. 2: “a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot”

- **Birth and death as the boundaries of life "under the sun."** These are the first pair, and both are fixed by God. As Gill puts it, a man does not come into the world at his own pleasure or another's, but at the will of God; the hour of death is likewise settled (citing Job 14:5). The seeds of mortality are in us from birth. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)
- **Planting and uprooting** may be understood literally (agriculture) or applied to the planting and plucking up of kingdoms (Jer 1:10), of Israel from the land, and even of Gospel churches. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)
- **Enduring Word** notes that "a bad facet answers each good facet" — the Preacher understood that the bad things in life cannot be escaped. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)

### v. 3: “a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to break down and a time to build”

- **"A time to kill"** is carefully distinguished from murder. The Hebrew word used is not the word for murder in the sixth commandment; it refers to lawful execution or killing in warfare. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)
- **Gill** notes it may refer to violent death in war, or execution by the civil magistrate; "heal" refers to recovery from wounds or sickness not appointed unto death. Spiritually, ministers slay souls by the law (the killing letter) and heal them by the Gospel. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)
- **Breaking down and building** may apply to cities (Jerusalem destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar and rebuilt under Nehemiah), and spiritually to the church — a time to break down and a time to restore (Amos 9:11). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)

### v. 4: “a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance”

- **Ellicott** notes that "mourn" is the ordinary Hebrew word for noisy funeral lamentations (Jer 4:8; 1 Sam 25:1). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/3.htm)
- **Gill** applies this to Israel weeping in Babylon and laughing at the return from captivity (Ps 137:1); to the church mourning in times of corruption and rejoicing in revival (Isa 61:3); and to individual believers who weep when Christ seems withdrawn and rejoice when He returns (Mt 9:15; Jn 16:19). The present state is the saints' weeping time; in the age to come they will laugh (Lk 6:21). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)

### v. 5: “a time to cast away stones and a time to gather stones together, a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing”

- **Casting away / gathering stones:** Ellicott says this refers to clearing or marring land (Isa 5:2; 2 Ki 3:19, 25) rather than building, since building is covered in v.3. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/3.htm)
- **Gill** adds it may also refer to throwing down buildings (the Temple, where not one stone was left upon another) and gathering the stones again. Spiritually, it may picture the Gentiles (stones) being gathered to become children of Abraham, and the Jews being cast away for rejecting Messiah then gathered again by conversion (Zech 9:16). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)
- **Embracing / refraining:** applies to conjugal embraces, parents embracing children, and friends embracing — all proper at times, but in calamitous seasons such fondness must be set aside. Spiritually, the embraces of Christ and believers are sometimes enjoyed, sometimes withdrawn (Prov 4:8). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)

### v. 6: “a time to search and a time to count as lost, a time to keep and a time to discard”

- **Ellicott** notes that the word translated "lose" elsewhere means "to destroy," but in later Hebrew it comes to mean "to lose" (like the Latin *perdere*). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/3.htm)
- **Gill** applies "search" and "lose" to God's seeking and saving the lost sheep of the house of Israel through Christ's redemption and the Spirit's effectual calling. "Keep and cast away" may refer to keeping riches (sometimes hoarded to the owner's harm) and scattering them among the poor, or casting goods overboard in a storm (Jonah 1:5; Acts 27). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)

### v. 7: “a time to tear and a time to mend, a time to be silent and a time to speak”

- **Tearing and mending:** Gill notes this refers to rending garments in mourning or at blasphemy, then sewing them up afterward. The Jews applied it to the rending of the ten tribes from Rehoboam (signified by the rending of Jeroboam's garment, 1 Ki 11:30) and their future reunification (Ezek 37:22). Some interpret it of the rending of the Jewish church state at Christ's death (the tearing of the veil) and the constitution of the Gentile church. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)
- **Silence and speech:** In an evil time (Amos 5:13), when a friend is in distress (Job 2:13), in the presence of scornful men (Ps 39:1), or under affliction (Lev 10:3), it is time to keep silence. Yet there is a time to speak publicly for the Gospel, to make open profession of Christ, and to pray and praise — "should they not, the stones in the wall would cry out." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)

### v. 8: “a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace”

- **Love and hate:** Gill explains there is a time to love a friend while he remains such, and to hate him (or love him less) when he proves treacherous — as with Amnon (2 Sam 13:15). In unregeneracy, a person loves worldly lusts and sinful pleasures; at conversion, there is a time to hate what was formerly loved. Even dearest relations are to be "hated" (loved less) in comparison with Christ. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)
- **War and peace:** The present Christian life is a warfare against sin, Satan, and the world; the future state is a time of peace, when saints will be no more disturbed by enemies. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)

### v. 9: “What does the worker gain from his toil?”

- This is the rhetorical question that follows from vv.1–8. **Gill** says: man has no profit from his labour since time is short, he leaves it to another he knows not who, and his life is attended with continual changes — sometimes one thing, sometimes its contrary. There is nothing certain or dependable under the sun without a divine blessing. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)
- **Enduring Word** notes that this time the Preacher finds an answer in "the God-given task" (v.10), unlike earlier when this question produced only despair. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)

### v. 10: “I have seen the burden that God has laid upon the sons of men to occupy them”

- The "burden" or "travail" is the painful toil of life. **Gill** says God's purpose is "to afflict" or "to humble" men by it — to let them see that all their labour signifies little, that all depends on a divine blessing, and that no happiness is found in the creatures. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)
- **Enduring Word** sees this as a significant shift: the Preacher now recognizes that there is a "God-given task" which the sons of men are to be occupied with. The question of v.9 now has an answer rooted in God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)

### v. 11: “He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end.”

- **"Everything beautiful in its time"**: This is a key turning point. God sees purpose and beauty in both the good *and* bad seasons of life. All things — prosperity and adversity, weeping and laughing — form a beautiful "checker work" in God's providential tapestry. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-3-commentary)
- **"Eternity in their hearts"**: This is one of the most discussed phrases in Ecclesiastes.
  - **Enduring Word** says we long for the eternal because we are made in the image of an eternal God. God has given us a yearning for the infinite, yet He has not fully revealed His eternal work — keeping that longing alive as an unfulfilled yearning. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)
  - **Ellicott** takes a distinctive approach: the Hebrew word translated "world" (or "eternity") in the KJV actually means "eternity" or "long duration" everywhere else in the Old Testament (over 300 occurrences). God has put in man's heart an expectation and longing for abiding continuance — so man fails to understand the changing seasons God ordains. Man wants things to last, but God ordains change. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/3.htm)
  - **John Piper** (Desiring God) says the verse means we long for a coherence to our own story and the world's story; this longing has been graciously gifted by God, but it takes the form of a "pained looking" because we cannot join up all the dots. The juxtaposition of time and eternity creates a jagged edge in human experience. The longing for more than this world can give points us to God. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/you-were-made-to-never-end)
  - **John MacArthur** (GTY) says the phrase means we have an inner sense of immortality, but God has not revealed His full plan; we must trust His sovereign timing in suffering and trials. (search excerpt from https://www.gty.org/blogs/B210118/life-under-the-sun)
- **Gill** notes that some render "the beautiful One" (the Messiah) has made all things in His time — the fair and lovely One who made all things in creation and works with the Father in providence and redemption. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)

### vv. 12–13: “I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and do good while they live, and also that every man should eat and drink and find satisfaction in all his labor—this is the gift of God.”

- **Enduring Word**: In light of God making everything beautiful and giving eternity in our hearts, it is wise to receive the good things of this life *as the gift of God*. Solomon briefly escapes his "under the sun" thinking. Michael Eaton calls this "holds out again hope of an enjoyable life from the hand of God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)
- **Ellicott** notes: "I know" — literally "I knew," i.e., "I came to know." The writer is relating conclusions at which he successively arrived. "To do good" is always used elsewhere in a moral sense ("to act rightly"), though the context may also suggest enjoyment. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/3.htm)
- **John MacArthur** adds: we need to recognize this life for the gift it is; in the short time we have, we don't need to be part of the disruption and rebellion. (search excerpt from GTY)

### vv. 14–15: “I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it. God does it so that they should fear Him. What exists has already been, and what will be has already been, for God will call to account what has passed.”

- **Enduring Word**: Here the Preacher escapes — ever so briefly — his "under the sun" thinking. Eaton highlights three aspects: God's actions are **permanent** (endure forever), **effective and complete** (nothing can be added), and **totally secure** (nothing taken from it). The proper human response is fear — not craven terror, but reverence and awesome regard for God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)
- **v.15 on God "requiring an account"**: Enduring Word says if God judges the heart and deeds of man, then everything has meaning. Kidner is quoted: "God has no abortive enterprises or forgotten men." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)
- **Ellicott** offers a different reading of v.15: the phrase "God requireth that which is past" is better rendered "God seeketh again" — i.e., God recalls the past. The writer has been speaking of the immutable order of the universe that constantly repeats itself. But the word suggesting "seeking for judgment" leads naturally to the next topic (v.16). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/3.htm)

### vv. 16–17: “Furthermore, I saw under the sun that in the place of judgment there is wickedness… I said in my heart, 'God will judge the righteous and the wicked, since there is a time for every activity and every deed.'”

- **Enduring Word**: Solomon looked at the here-and-now world and saw that instead of fair judgment there was wickedness, and instead of righteousness, iniquity. This is a significant problem: if there is no eternity, the wicked often win and the righteous lose. The Preacher "perhaps hoped" that God would judge — not only in this life but beyond. Because there is a time for every purpose, God will judge deeds to see if they fit the proper purpose. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)
- **Ellicott** says this verse clearly speaks of a judgment after this life, "but not yet asserted as a conclusion definitely adopted, but only as a belief of the writer's conflicting with the doubts expressed in the following verses." The phrase "I said in my heart" (used in both vv.17 and 18) conveys "I thought — and yet again I thought," showing the writer's internal debate. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/3.htm)

### vv. 18–19: “I said to myself, 'As for the sons of men, God tests them so that they may see for themselves that they are but beasts.' For the fates of both men and beasts are the same… man has no advantage over the animals, since everything is futile.”

- **Enduring Word**: This is strictly "under the sun" thinking — looking at life and death absent any eternal perspective. By all outward appearance, humans and animals die the same way and their bodies decompose identically. Deane notes the emphatic pronoun: "that *they themselves* are [like] beasts, *they in themselves*." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)
- **Enduring Word** explicitly rejects using this as an argument for annihilationism, for two reasons: (1) Solomon is speaking as a man unconvinced of eternity; (2) the New Testament (2 Tim 1:10) reveals that Jesus "brought life and immortality to light through the gospel" — the afterlife is cloudy in the OT but clear in the NT. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)
- **Ellicott** renders "breath" as the same Hebrew word as "spirit" in v.21 (Gen 7:15; Ps 104:30). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/3.htm)

### vv. 20–21: “All go to one place; all come from dust, and all return to dust. Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal descends into the earth?”

- **Enduring Word**: We sense the Preacher *hoped* there was a different destiny for humans and animals, but in his "under the sun" thinking there was no real reason to believe it — hence, "Who knows?" The Teacher is "speaking phenomenologically, i.e., as things appear to the senses" (Wright). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)
- **Ellicott** notes that the LXX and a great body of interpreters ancient and modern translate v.21 as "Who knoweth *whether* the spirit of man goeth upward?" — a genuinely sceptical question, not a statement of doubt overcome. The sceptical thought is: we see the body return to dust for both; can anyone claim with certainty to know what happens to the spirit? The writer seems to have read both Psalm 49:14 and Proverbs 15:24. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/3.htm)

### v. 22: “I have seen that there is nothing better for a man than to enjoy his work, because that is his lot. For who can bring him to see what will come after him?”

- **Enduring Word**: After briefly flirting with confidence in eternity (vv.9–15), the Preacher returns to his "under the sun" thinking. Under that premise, nothing is better than to accomplish what one can in this world and not trouble oneself about what comes after — because, from that perspective, death ends it all and human life has no more meaning than an animal's. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)
- The Preacher is not endorsing this as final truth; he is reporting the best conclusion available *without* eternity in view.

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed / Calvinist (Desiring God — John Piper)
Piper reads the chapter as underscoring God's absolute sovereignty over time and events. The "eternity in the heart" (v.11) is a God-given longing that *frustrates* us with this world so that we turn to God. He famously links it to C.S. Lewis: "If we find ourselves with a desire that nothing in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that we were made for another world." Boredom itself is God's pointer to eternity. Piper also stresses that we cannot control events, relationships, or ultimate outcomes — God alone does. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/you-were-made-to-never-end; https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/gods-purpose-in-our-boredom)

### Baptist / Particular Baptist (Gill)
Gill's approach is heavily providential and typological. He sees every pair of opposites as part of God's eternal decree and applies many of them directly to the history of Israel, the church, and the work of Christ (e.g., "planting and plucking up" applied to Israel's exile and restoration; "killing and healing" to the law and Gospel; "casting away stones" to the calling of the Gentiles and future conversion of the Jews). His reading is thoroughly Christological — v.11 even notes that some render the phrase as "the beautiful One" (the Messiah) making all things. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-3.html)

### Evangelical / Dispensational (Grace to You — John MacArthur)
MacArthur sees the book as Solomon's painful autobiography — writing in his latter years to warn the young. The key word is "vanity," expressing the futility of seeking satisfaction apart from God. MacArthur views v.11 as teaching that we won't always know what God is accomplishing through suffering; we must trust His sovereign timing. The "enjoy life" theme is tethered to divine judgment: the only fulfilled life is one lived in proper recognition of God. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/1249/you-only-live-twice; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/macarthur_john/bible-introductions/ecclesiastes-intro.cfm)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik)
Guzik traces the movement from the oppressive monotony of time (vv.1–8) through glimpses of hope (vv.9–15) and back to "under the sun" despair (vv.16–22). The chapter is seen as an honest internal struggle rather than settled doctrine. The list of opposites is read as "the monotony of all things, rather than their variety" (Morgan). Hope comes in recognising God as the master of time and in the gift of "eternity in our hearts." The famous song "Turn! Turn! Turn!" by the Byrds is noted (via Precept Austin) as popularising the passage. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-3/)

### Anglican / Older Commentary (Ellicott)
Ellicott stands out for his careful lexical notes and his reading of the chapter as an unresolved internal debate. He emphasises that v.17 speaks of judgment after death but only as a belief conflicting with the doubts of vv.18–21 — not yet a settled conclusion. On v.15 he differs from most by reading "God requires an account" as "God recalls the past" (the cyclical repetition of history). On v.21, he sides with the LXX reading that makes it a genuinely sceptical question: "Who knows *whether* the spirit of man goes upward?" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/3.htm)

## Other Views and Missing Traditions

**I was unable to access** the following due to search and fetch limits in this session. The user may wish to pursue these separately:

- **Lutheran** (lcms.org, 1517.org) — no results returned.
- **Methodist / Wesleyan** (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com) — not reached.
- **Catholic** (newadvent.org, catholic.com) — the Catholic tradition typically reads Ecclesiastes 3 in light of natural law and the Catechism's teaching on the afterlife; v.21 is often cited regarding the immortality of the soul versus animal mortality. Not accessed in this session.
- **Orthodox** (oca.org) — the Orthodox reading often emphasises the liturgical use of this passage and the hope of resurrection. Not accessed.
- **Modern scholarship** (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) — NET Bible notes were cited second-hand via Precept Austin (noting the balance between divine sovereignty and human responsibility in vv.1–8 vs. 9–15). The full NET notes were not fetched.
- **Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-grace** — no relevant results from approved sites. Some prosperity teachers have used vv.12–13 to argue that God wants believers to enjoy material abundance, but no source from the approved list was found making or critiquing this claim.
